title: Functions II
subtitle: Spells You Can Hand Over
martuIntro:
You know recipes. Now they read stat sheets, write spell books, and guard the door. And one more thing, the strange one: a recipe can sit in a box, like any value. You can hand it to someone without cooking it.
You have seen all of this in the campaign: `get_mana_bar(caster)`, `add_spell(...)` with `strengthen_magic` and no `()`, and `cast_spell` holding the barrier. A lot of that code felt like a wall, yes? This unit takes the wall apart. By the end, it is your code.
goals: Write a recipe (a function) that takes a hero's whole stat sheet and hands back a line built from it
Change a sheet inside a function, and know when a function needs `return` and when it doesn't
Build a spell from a function's parameters, with keys that match them letter for letter, and store it in a spell book by its name
Stop a function early with `return` when something is wrong, like a spell the hero doesn't know
Read the `def` line of a finished helper, call it the right way, and leave it as it is
Keep what one function hands back in a variable, then pass it on to another: build the bar, then draw it
Keep a function in a variable or a dictionary, hand it over without `()`, and call it later, like the campaign's spell book

items.title: Recipes That Read Stat Sheets
items.summary: Write functions that read and change a hero's stat sheet. Build spells from parameters, guard the door, and call helpers you didn't write.

exercises.title: Hand a function a whole sheet
exercises.martu:
In Unit 3 you wrote recipes. Python calls a recipe a [[functions|function]], and from now on so do we. A function can take a whole stat sheet as one [[parameter]] (Unit 3's ingredient). It's like x in f(x) in math: x stands for any number, and `hero` stands for any sheet. `mana_line(lucky)` puts Lucky's sheet in `hero`, so `hero["mana"]` reads 20.
Inside the function, read the sheet by key, as in Unit 5: the name, the mana (magic power) and the max mana (the most mana the hero can hold). Then hand the line back with `return`, so `print(...)` at the bottom gets it.
Right now the function only says `pass`. Press Run first and see what shows, yes?

anotherWay.label: One function, two sheets
anotherWay.text:
```text
mana_line(lucky)
  hero = Lucky's sheet
  -> "Lucky: 20/26"
mana_line(oogrish)
  hero = Oogrish's sheet
  -> "Oogrish: 18/18"
```
The same steps run each time. The call decides which sheet `hero` holds.

1. The call hands over a sheet, and `hero` holds it.
2. `hero["name"]` reads the name.
3. `str(hero["mana"])` and `str(hero["max_mana"])` turn the numbers into text.
4. `+` glues the pieces, with `": "` and `"/"` between them.
5. `return` hands the line back to the call.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: In the mana bars, `get_mana_bar(caster)` took a caster's whole sheet, read `caster["mana"]` and `caster["max_mana"]`, and returned the bar as text. The game handed in each party member's sheet. `mana_line(hero)` has the same shape.

anotherWay.label: From English class
anotherWay.text: A function with a sheet is like a sentence frame in English class: `____: ____/____`. Each call fills the blanks from a different sheet: `Lucky: 20/26` from Lucky's, `Oogrish: 18/18` from Oogrish's.

anotherWay.text: Try *Variables inside a function stay there*, in the lesson Extra practice: Defaults and Scope. A variable made inside a function vanishes when the function ends. It comes back out only if the function returns it.

campaignLink.why: You have seen this. `get_mana_bar(caster)` took a whole sheet as one parameter, read it by key, and returned text. The game called it for every party member. `mana_line` works the same way.

exercises.takeaway: A function can take a whole sheet as one parameter: `def mana_line(hero):`. It reads the sheet by key and can `return` the line it builds.

predict.q: Before you press Run: the function only says `pass`. What will this show?
predict.explain: A function with no `return` hands back `None`, Python's word for nothing. `print` shows that `None`. Your `return` line will give the call a real line to show.

exercises.title: Functions can change a sheet
exercises.martu:
When you hand a function a sheet, it gets [[same sheet|that very sheet]], not a copy. So a change the function makes shows up for the line that called it. It's like sharing a Google Doc instead of handing out a printed copy: your friend's edits show up in your doc. `rest(lucky)` writes into `hero["mana"]`, and Lucky's own sheet fills up.
Look at `rest(hero)` at the top of your code. It returns nothing. Press Run: after `rest(lucky)`, Lucky's mana is full anyway.
So when does a function need `return`? When the line that called it needs a value back, like `mana_line`. A function that only changes a sheet, like `rest`, doesn't. Remember this rule, yes?

anotherWay.label: Why does this work? One sheet, two names
anotherWay.text:
```text
lucky --+
        +--> {"mana": 9 ...}
hero  --+
```
During the call, `lucky` and `hero` are two names for one sheet. `hero["mana"] = 26` changes that sheet, so `lucky["mana"]` shows 26 after. Nothing was copied, so nothing has to be returned.
Like handing someone your notebook, not a photo of it. Whatever they write in it is there when you get it back.

1. `spend(lucky, 4)`: `hero` is Lucky's sheet, `cost` is 4.
2. The right side reads `hero["mana"]`, 26, and takes 4 away: 22.
3. The left side writes 22 into `hero["mana"]`, which is Lucky's sheet.
4. The function ends. `lucky["mana"]` is 22.
Need a value back? `return` it. Changing the sheet? Write into it by key. No `return` is needed.

exercises.title: Build a spell from parameters
exercises.martu:
A function can build a dictionary from its parameters, using [[matching parameter|matching]] names. Each key gets the parameter with the same name, letter for letter. It's like quotation marks in English class: `"mana_cost"` in quotes means the key's exact letters. With no quotes, `mana_cost` means look inside the parameter, at the cost that was handed in. So `"mana_cost": mana_cost` is a match.
The campaign said it like this: *replace each placeholder with the matching parameter*.
Then `return` the spell, so the line that called the function can keep it.

anotherWay.label: Same word, two jobs
anotherWay.text:
Try it if you like (it's not a step):
1. Rename the parameter `mana_cost` to `cost`, on the `def` line and after the colon. Press Run: it still works.
2. Now rename the key `"mana_cost"` to `"cost"`. Press Run: the spell changes shape.
`"mana_cost"` with quotes is a key. `mana_cost` without quotes holds the value handed in. Put both back when you are done.

anotherWay.label: Where each value goes
anotherWay.text:
```text
make_spell(5, 2, "teal")
  mana_cost         = 5
  required_affinity = 2
  color             = "teal"
spell:
  "mana_cost": 5
  "required_affinity": 2
  "color": "teal"
```

1. The call hands over three values, in order.
2. They land in the parameters, in the same order as the `def` line.
3. Each key gets the parameter with its own name.
4. `return spell` hands the finished spell back to the call.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: In the spell book you replaced `"mana_cost": 0` with `"mana_cost": mana_cost`, the matching parameter. The game later read exactly `spell["mana_cost"]`, so a near name like `"cost"` would have broken it.

exercises.title: Store by name
exercises.martu:
A spell book is a dictionary of spells: each key is a spell's name, and its value is the spell. It's like the glossary at the back of a textbook, where you look a word up by the word itself. `book[spell_name] = spell` adds one spell. `spell_name` has no quotes, so the key is whatever name was handed in, like `"Glow"`.
A function gets the very book it is handed, the same idea as the sheet in `spend`. Store into it, and the book outside the function gets the new spell too. `book = {...}` makes a new book instead, and the book outside never changes.

anotherWay.label: Why does this work? Why `book = {...}` doesn't reach the book outside

anotherWay.text: A library shelf with name cards. `book[spell_name] = spell` slides a new spell in behind its own name card. `book = {...}` builds a whole new shelf in another room, and nobody at the old shelf sees it.

1. `add_to_book(lucky_book, "Glow", glow)`: `book` is Lucky's book, `spell_name` is `"Glow"`, `spell` is the glow spell.
2. `book[spell_name] = spell` makes the key `"Glow"` and puts the spell under it.
3. The function ends. `lucky_book` now holds Glow.

exercises.title: Guard at the door
exercises.martu:
A [[guard]] is an `if` at the top of a function that checks first. If something is wrong, it shows a line and stops the function with `return`, so nothing below it runs. It's like a form that says "Stop here if you are under 13": you don't fill in the rest. In the Example, `if name not in guests:` is the guard.
Press Run first. Lucky tries a spell he doesn't know, and Python stops with a [[KeyError]].
Your guard goes at the top of `cast_glow`, above the line that reads the spell. It has three lines: an `if`, the line it shows, then `return`. A good guard does not argue, yes?

anotherWay.text: A guard checks your name at the door before anything else happens. Not on the list? You hear why, and that is the end of it. On the list? In you go.

1. `cast_glow(lucky, "Star Glow")`: `spell_name` is `"Star Glow"`.
2. The guard asks: is `"Star Glow"` not in Lucky's book? Yes, it is not.
3. It shows `Lucky doesn't know Star Glow.`
4. `return` ends the function. The spell line never runs, so no KeyError.

anotherWay.label: Why does this work? `return` is `break` for a whole function
anotherWay.text: In Unit 6, `break` stopped a loop early. `return` stops a whole function early. Everything after it is skipped, so the guard needs no `else`.

exercises.title: Read the helper
exercises.martu:
A [[helpers|helper]] is a finished function that someone else wrote for you to call. You use it without changing it, the way you press a calculator's √ key without opening the calculator. Your job is to *read* its `def` line and call it right. `draw_bar(hero, bar)` means: hand over a hero's sheet first, then the bar text.
The `#` notes inside say what it does. Leave its lines alone, and write your call at the bottom.
In the campaign, `print_mana(caster, mana_bar)` was a helper like this one.

anotherWay.label: Two quick questions
anotherWay.text:
Which lines of `draw_bar` should you change? None: it is finished.
What two things does it need? A hero's sheet, then the bar text, in that order.

1. Read the `def` line: `hero`, then `bar`.
2. Match each one to something you have: `lucky` for `hero`, your text for `bar`.
3. Write the call in that order, at the bottom: `draw_bar(lucky, "███░")`.
4. Run. The helper does the rest.
Like a vending machine: you don't open it up. You read the label, put in what it asks for, in the order it asks, and press the button.

anotherWay.label: From math class
anotherWay.text: A point (x, y) is always x first, then y: (3, 5) and (5, 3) are different points. A call works the same way. `draw_bar(lucky, "███░")` puts the sheet first and the bar second, in the order of the `def` line.

exercises.martu:
*Store, then pass*, as in Unit 3: keep what one function returns in a variable, then hand that variable to another function. It's like a math problem with two parts: you write down the answer to part a, then use it in part b. `fuel_bar = get_fuel_bar(robot)` keeps the bar, and `draw_bar(robot, fuel_bar)` passes it on.
Gearshift's fuel gauge works like the mana bars. `get_fuel_bar` builds the bar, and a finished helper draws it. The numbered `#` notes match your steps, one each. The blocks `▮` and `▯` are already typed.

anotherWay.label: Who hands what to whom
anotherWay.text:
```text
show_fuel(gearshift)
  fuel_bar = get_fuel_bar(robot)
      -> "Fuel [▮▮▮▮▯▯] 4/6"
  draw_bar(robot, fuel_bar)
      -> the row on screen
```

1. The loop at the bottom hands each robot to `show_fuel`.
2. `show_fuel` calls `get_fuel_bar(robot)` and stores the bar.
3. `get_fuel_bar` makes the full blocks, then the light ones, and returns the bar as text.
4. `show_fuel` passes the robot and the stored bar to `draw_bar`, which draws the row.
Like a baker and a shop window. The baker makes the cake and hands it over. You carry it, then set it in the window. You never put the baker in the window.

predict.explain: Python does `*` before `-`, as in PEMDAS. It makes `▯▯▯▯▯` first, then tries to take 3 away from text, and stops. Parentheses go first: `"▯" * (5 - 3)` makes `▯▯`.

exercises.title: Broken spell
exercises.martu:
This code has four [[bug|bugs]]. Three are loud: each one makes Python stop with an error. One is quiet: no error, and the Console even looks right, like writing *their* for *there*, which spell-check doesn't catch. *Mend* means fix. Python shows one error at a time, so fix one, press Run again, and see what Python finds next.
When Python stops, read the box in the Console, in this order:
1. Read its title. It says what went wrong.
2. Read *Python's last line*. It says the same thing in Python's words.
3. Find the line number. If that line calls a function, the bug may be inside the function.
The quiet bug comes last. My checks find it, yes?

anotherWay.label: One bug at a time
anotherWay.text:
1. Press Run. Read the box in the Console: its title, then Python's last line.
2. Find the line number. If that line calls a function, the bug may be inside the function.
3. Fix it and press Run again. A new error? Good: Python got further, to the next bug.
4. No error? The checks tell you what is left.

items.title: Spells You Can Hand Over
items.summary: Keep a function in a variable, hand it to another function with no `()`, store it in a dictionary, then write the spell book and cast from it.

exercises.title: A name without parentheses
exercises.martu:
The name of a [[function]] with no `()` is the function itself: a recipe card, not the meal. A variable can hold it, like any value. `chosen_spell = warm_hands` puts the card in a box, and nothing runs. It's like f(x) in math class, as in Unit 3: f is the rule, and f(13) works it out. `warm_hands` is the rule, and `warm_hands(lucky)` runs it.
Later, `chosen_spell(lucky)` runs what the variable holds. The parentheses `()` are what call it.
In Unit 3, a recipe's name on a line by itself did nothing. Now you know why: the name is the function itself.

anotherWay.label: A box holding a recipe card
anotherWay.text:
```text
chosen_spell = warm_hands
  box: [card: warm_hands]
  nothing runs yet

chosen_spell(lucky)
  the card is cooked now
  Lucky warms up.

chosen_spell = warm_hands(lucky)
  warm_hands runs NOW
  box: None
```

Handing someone a recipe card is not the same as cooking the meal and handing them the empty pot. `warm_hands` is the card. `warm_hands(lucky)` cooks it now, and what comes back is the empty pot, `None`.

1. `def warm_hands(hero):` makes the function. Nothing runs.
2. `chosen_spell = warm_hands` puts the same function in a second variable. Nothing runs.
3. `chosen_spell(lucky)` runs it, with `lucky` as `hero`.
4. The Console shows `Lucky warms up.`

anotherWay.label: Why does this work? Two names, one function
anotherWay.text: A function's name points at the function, the way a variable's name points at its value. `chosen_spell = warm_hands` gives the same function a second name, like a nickname. Either name can call it.
In Unit 3, `barrier_report` on a line by itself did nothing and gave no error. Now you know why: the name is the function itself. Only `()` runs it.

anotherWay.label: Cook it too early on purpose
anotherWay.text: Try it if you like (it's not a step). After both steps show ✓, change line 13 to `chosen_spell = warm_hands(lucky)` and press Run. Read the box in the Console, then Python's last line: `chosen_spell` holds `None` now, and `None` can't be called. Then change line 13 back.

exercises.title: Hand it over
exercises.martu:
You can hand a function to another function, [[function as a value|like any value]]. It's the recipe card again: you hand a cook the card and a list of guests, and the cook follows the card once for each guest. `cast_on_everyone(roster, warm_hands)` hands over the list and the card, `warm_hands`, with no `()`.
`cast_on_everyone(heroes, effect)` is already written. Its parameter `effect` is a blank, like the blanks in Unit 3's sentence frames. For each hero, it calls `effect(hero)`. It doesn't know which spell `effect` is. You choose when you call it.
With `()`, the function would run once, right now, and `cast_on_everyone` would get `None` instead of the function.
`roster` holds the four heroes. It is already made.

example.output:
The moth nods.
Captain Glug nods.

anotherWay.label: Handing over the card
anotherWay.text:
```text
cast_on_everyone(roster,
                 warm_hands)

inside: effect = warm_hands
  Oogrish:    effect(hero)
  Gearshift:  effect(hero)
  Bomb Shell: effect(hero)
  Lucky:      effect(hero)
```
You hand over the card once. The loop cooks it four times.
You hand a cook a recipe card and a list of guests. The cook makes the dish once for each guest. If you cooked it yourself first and handed over the empty pot, the cook would have nothing to follow.

1. `cast_on_everyone(roster, warm_hands)`: `heroes` holds `roster`, `effect` holds `warm_hands`.
2. The loop takes the first hero. `effect(hero)` runs `warm_hands` on Oogrish.
3. Then Gearshift, Bomb Shell and Lucky.
4. Your `cool_down` works the same way: hand it over, and the loop runs it.

exercises.title: A recipe in a box
exercises.martu:
A dictionary can hold a function as a value, like a recipe card filed in a recipe box. In `glow`, the key `"effect"` holds `light_lantern`, with no `()`. `glow["effect"]` takes the card out. Add `(lucky)` on the end, and the function runs: `glow["effect"](lucky)`.
Read it left to right, like a sentence: the dictionary, the key in square brackets, then the parentheses that call it. `glow["effect"]` on its own only reads the function. Nothing runs.
A spell book is a dictionary of pages, one page for each spell, as in Unit 5. From a book, read the page by its name first, then the key, then call it.

```text
lucky_book["Glow"]     the page
lucky_book["Glow"]["effect"]
                       the card
lucky_book["Glow"]["effect"](lucky)
                       cook it
```

exercises.title: Write the spell book
exercises.martu:
[[None]] is Python's word for *nothing here yet*. It holds a spot, like a blank line on a form you fill in later. It is not 0: 0 is a number, and `None` is no value at all. In `spell`, `"effect": None` holds the spot where a function will go.
`learn_spell` builds a spell, then stores it in a hero's book. Replace each placeholder (`0`, `0` and `None`) with the matching parameter: the one with exactly the key's name. Then store the spell by its name.
The given loop gives every hero Lantern Ward, a ward: a spell that protects. Its `lantern_ward` has no `()`: the ward is handed over, not cast. The last line shows `False` until your store works.

anotherWay.label: Each key, its matching parameter
anotherWay.text:
```text
key (quotes)   value (no quotes)
"mana_cost"  <- mana_cost
"required_affinity"
             <- required_affinity
"effect"     <- effect

spell_book[spell_name] = spell
  the page's name: no quotes
```

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: This is `add_spell()`. You replaced each placeholder with the matching parameter, then wrote `spell_book[spell_name] = spell`. The campaign's `"spell_function"` is our `"effect"`.

1. The loop calls `learn_spell(hero["spell_book"], "Lantern Ward", 6, 9, lantern_ward)`.
2. Inside, `mana_cost` holds 6, `required_affinity` holds 9, `effect` holds `lantern_ward`.
3. `spell` is built from those parameters.
4. `spell_book[spell_name] = spell` writes the page into the hero's own book.

anotherWay.label: Why does this work? The book outside changes
anotherWay.text: `spell_book` is not a copy. It is the hero's own book, handed in. A change by key reaches the book outside the function, as in Store by name. Only `spell_book = {...}` would point the name at a new, empty book.

anotherWay.label: From math class
anotherWay.text: In math, 0 is a number: 0 + 5 is 5. `None` is not a number. It's like an empty answer box on a worksheet: nothing is written there yet. In Python, `None + 5` makes Python stop with an error.

exercises.martu:
The campaign's barrier spell, rebuilt. `cast` works in three parts: *get it, compare, act*. *Get it* is done: the guard checks that the hero knows the spell, then `spell` holds its page. You write the rest with `if`, `elif` and `else`, like a grading scale from Unit 2: Python checks from the top and stops at the first True.

2. Otherwise, if the hero's mana (magic power) is lower than the cost, say so.
3. Otherwise, cast: call `spell["effect"](hero)`, pay the cost, and show the bar.

exercises.title: Broken spell
exercises.martu:
Bomb Shell copied the spell book and the barrier from memory, and made four mistakes: four [[bug|bugs]]. In the last broken spell, most bugs were loud: Python stopped. These four are all quiet: the code runs, but does the wrong thing, like typing *their* for *there*.
Press Run and read the first lines in the Console. The wards glow before anyone casts. That's a clue, yes?
*Mend* means fix. Fix one bug, then press Run again. I also test `cast` with other heroes.

anotherWay.label: One bug at a time
anotherWay.text:
1. Press Run. Read the Console: what happened, and in what order?
2. An error box? Read its title, then Python's last line. Find the line number and fix that line.
3. No error? Compare what you see with what should happen. The checks tell you what is left.
4. Fix one bug, then press Run again.

```text
lantern_ward(hero)

spell["effect"]

  is turned away
hero["mana"] - cost
  quiet: worked out,
  then forgotten
```

items.title: Spell Recipes Quiz
items.summary: Quiz: 8 questions on functions as values, changing a sheet, an early `return` and the spell book. Retake it as often as you like.

questions.q: What will this print?
questions.explain: `spells["glow"]` reads the function `glow` out of the dictionary. `("Lucky")` calls it, and it hands back `"Lucky glows."`. The `print` shows what came back.

questions.q: Which line hands `warm_hands` to `cast_on_everyone` without running it?

whyWrong.1: With `()`, `warm_hands` runs right now, before `cast_on_everyone` starts. No hero is handed over yet, so Python stops with an error: *missing 1 required positional argument*.
whyWrong.2: In quotes it is only text. `cast_on_everyone` would try to call the text, and Python stops: *'str' object is not callable*.

questions.explain: The name with no `()` is the function itself. `cast_on_everyone` calls it later, once for each hero, with `effect(hero)`.

questions.q: What will this print?
questions.explain: `hero` and `lucky` are two names for the same sheet, not two copies. So the change inside the function reaches `lucky`: 26 - 3 = 23. No `return` is needed for that.

questions.q: Put the lines in order, with their indents. The program should show `Lucky is safe.`, then `No: Moss`. Lucky has exactly enough mana to cast Glow, and Moss does not.
questions.explain: `<` lets exactly enough mana cast: 6 is not lower than 6, so Lucky is safe. Moss has 3, which is lower, so the `if` turns Moss away. In the `else`, `spell["effect"](hero)` reads the function from the dictionary and calls it. Without `(hero)`, nothing would happen.

questions.q: Put the lines in order, with their indents. `learn_spell` builds a spell and stores it by name, so the program shows `{'Glow': {'mana_cost': 2}}`.
questions.explain: The value is the parameter `cost`, with no quotes. The key is the parameter `name`, with no quotes. `book[name] = spell` changes the book handed in; `book = {...}` would only make a new one inside.

questions.q: This program stops with a TypeError. Fix it so it shows 3 full blocks, then 2 empty ones: `███░░`.
questions.explain: It's PEMDAS: Python does `*` before `-`. Without parentheses it makes five blocks, then tries to take a number away from text, and stops. Parentheses make it subtract first: `"░" * (max_mana - mana)`.

questions.q: What does the `return` on line 3 do, with nothing after it?
choices: It ends the function right there. The line that called gets `None`.
It goes back to the top of the function.
Nothing: the next line still runs.

whyWrong.1: A `return` with nothing after it returns nothing: `None`. To return the mana, it would need `return hero["mana"]`.
whyWrong.2: `return` never loops. It leaves the function.
whyWrong.3: The function stops at `return`. The `print` below it runs only when the `if` was false.

questions.explain: `return` ends the function at once. With nothing after it, the line that called gets `None`. That is how a guard works: it stops the function early.

questions.q: What will this print?
choices:
Unknown: Mist
Casting Mist
Casting Glow
questions.explain: Mist is not in the book, so the guard prints `Unknown: Mist` and `return` ends that call. The second call knows Glow, so it goes past the guard: `Casting Glow`.

items.title: The Resonance Array
items.summary: Project: write the dials of Mar'tu's brass machine as functions, use them to measure a hero, and run the machine with a dial handed over.
items.intro:
Mar'tu brought a brass machine from the Institute: the resonance array. It has dials, and each dial is a function with a formula, like the formulas in math class.
Three parts, in order, matching the notes `# A.`, `# B.` and `# C.` in your code: A. write the dials, B. calibrate a hero (work out both readings for one hero), C. run the array.
`roster` holds the four heroes:
```text
name        affinity  die
Oogrish         9      d6
Gearshift      10      d8
Bomb Shell     12      d8
Lucky          13      d6
```
Their keys are `"name"`, `"magical_affinity"` and `"die_size"`.
Tasks 1 to 5 print nothing: the Console stays empty until Task 6 runs the array. Each Done line says what Mar'tu tested.
items.martu:
Each dial is a function. It gets its numbers through its parameters when it is called, and hands the answer back with `return`. It's a formula, like in math class: area = length × width works for any rectangle, and `return length * width` works for any call. I test your dials with other numbers and other heroes, so a typed-in answer won't work.
Two dials at the bottom, `mana_dial` and `damage_dial`, are finished. Read them, use them, and leave them as they are.
At the Institute we wrote every dial as a recipe. Then nobody argued about the math.

anotherWay.label: The array
anotherWay.text:
```text
 dials (functions)
   max_mana_for  affinity -> mana
   average_damage die -> damage
        |
 calibrate(hero)
   -> {"max_mana": ...,
       "average_damage": ...}
        |
 run_array(roster, mana_dial)
   one reading per hero
```

1. A dial: replace `return 0` with the formula, using the parameters.
2. `calibrate`: read two numbers from `hero`, hand each to its dial, and hand both back in a dictionary.
3. `run_array`: a loop over `heroes`, printing `dial(hero)`.
4. Hand `mana_dial` over with no `()`.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: `get_mana_bar(caster)` read a sheet and handed back a value, and `show_mana(caster)` passed it on. `calibrate` reads a sheet too. `run_array` takes a function, like `add_spell` took `strengthen_magic`.

anotherWay.label: From math class
anotherWay.text: A dial is a function, like f(x) = x + 3 in math class. f(7) puts 7 in for x and gives back 10. A dial call works the same way: the number in the parentheses goes in for the parameter, and `return` hands the answer back. One difference: Python needs `*` for times, so write `3 * x`, never `3x`.

items.title: The Spell Book, From Blank
items.summary: Optional challenge: write `learn_spell` and `cast` from a blank page. The spell book and the barrier, every line yours.
items.martu:
The spell book and the barrier, from a blank page. You've written every piece already. Now put them together, the way an essay grows from an outline. Write two functions:
1. `learn_spell(spell_book, spell_name, mana_cost, required_affinity, effect)` builds `spell` from the matching parameters, then stores it in `spell_book` under `spell_name`.
2. `cast(hero, spell_name)` asks the book first: a name it doesn't hold gets a message and `return`. Then get the page, compare, act: too little affinity, then too little mana, each says so; otherwise cast the effect, pay the cost, and call `show_mana(hero)`.
Write them above the three test lines. To try one, take off its `#` and the space after it. `roster`, `lantern_ward` and `show_mana` are already made. I also test with other heroes and spells.

anotherWay.label: The campaign's order
anotherWay.text:
1. `learn_spell`: build `spell` from the matching parameters.
2. Store it: the book, by the name.
3. `cast`: ask the book with `not in`; a message, then `return`.
4. Get the page. Compare the affinity, then the mana, with `<`.
5. `else`: cast, pay, show.

anotherWay.label: Two functions, one book
anotherWay.text:
```text
learn_spell(book, name, ...)
  spell = {...}
  book[name] = spell

cast(hero, name)
  name not in book?
    -> say so, return
  spell = the page
  affinity low? -> not skilled
  mana low? -----> need mana
  else: cast, pay, show
```

anotherWay.text: These are `add_spell` and `cast_spell`, with our names. In the lesson you filled them in: the placeholders, the store, the branches. Here the page starts blank, and every line is yours.

items.title: Extra practice: Defaults and Scope
items.summary: Optional practice. Give a parameter a usual value, and name a value in a call. Then see why a variable made inside a function can't be seen outside it.

exercises.title: Default values and named values
exercises.martu:
A [[default value]] is the usual value for a parameter, used when the call hands over nothing. You met one in Unit 4: `chalk_wall[:3]` leaves the start empty, so Python starts at 0. Write a default on the `def` line with `=`: `def roll_die(die_size=20):`. Then `roll_die()` rolls a d20, a die with 20 sides. `roll_die(6)` hands over 6, and the 6 wins.
You can also name the value in a call: `roll_die(die_size=6)`. Python calls that a [[keyword argument]]. It's like naming numbers in math class: "y = 3, x = 2" is the same point as "x = 2, y = 3", because each number has its name.
Press Run first. Python stops, because `roll_die()` hands over nothing yet.

anotherWay.label: A value already filled in
anotherWay.text:
```text
def roll_die(die_size=20):
             ^^^^^^^^^^^^
         used when the
         call is empty

roll_die()           20
roll_die(6)          6
roll_die(die_size=6) 6
```

anotherWay.label: Your phone's default ringtone
anotherWay.text: Your phone plays its default ringtone until you pick another one. A default value works the same way: Python uses it until a call hands over a value of its own.

1. `def roll_die(die_size=20):` gives `die_size` a default.
2. `roll_die()` hands over nothing, so `die_size` is 20.
3. `roll_die(die_size=6)` names the value, so `die_size` is 6.
4. Inside, `random.randint(1, die_size)` rolls whichever die it got.

anotherWay.text: In the skill checks, every call to `perform_roll(die_size)` had to say which die. With `die_size=20` on the `def` line, a plain `perform_roll()` would roll a d20.

exercises.title: Variables inside a function stay there
exercises.martu:
A variable made inside a function, like `restored`, exists only inside that function, and only while it runs. Its parameters, like `hero`, do too. Python calls this [[scope]]. It's like scratch paper in math class: you work on it, but only the answer sheet gets handed in. `return restored` puts the value on the answer sheet.
So the last line, `print(restored)`, is outside `rest`, and Python stops there. To get the value out, `rest` must hand it back with [[return]], and the line outside catches it in a variable of its own: `gained = rest(lucky)`.
The sheet is different. `hero` is another name for Lucky's own sheet, so the refill changes Lucky's mana. That part needs no `return`.

anotherWay.label: Inside and outside
anotherWay.text:
```text
rest's kitchen        outside
  hero                 lucky
  restored             gained
     |                  ^
     +-- return ------+
```
Only `return` passes a value through the wall.

anotherWay.label: The baker's counter
anotherWay.text: A baker weighs the flour on a scale in the back room. You never see the scale. You get the bread over the counter. `restored` is the scale, and `return` is the counter.

1. `rest(lucky)` starts: `hero` is Lucky's sheet.
2. `full` is 26, and `restored` is 26 - 20 = 6.
3. Lucky's mana becomes 26.
4. `return restored` hands back 6, and the variables inside `rest` are cleared away.
5. `gained = ...` catches the 6.
Unit 3 asked: whose kitchen is `result` in? Same answer here. A variable made in a function belongs to that function. The line that called gets only what is handed back.

items.title: lambda: A Function in One Line
items.summary: Optional article. Write a whole function on one line, like `lambda hero: hero["mana"]`. Store it, or hand it straight over.
items.body:
Some functions are tiny: one line, used once, handed straight to another function. For those, Python has a short form, the [[lambda]]. It's like a rule in math class, n → n ÷ 2: take n, hand back half. `//` ([[floor division]], from Unit 1's Clock Math) divides and drops any remainder, so `7 // 2` is 3, not 3.5.
```python
half = lambda n: n // 2
```
That's a whole function. Before the colon is the parameter, `n`. After the colon is what it hands back. There's no `def` and no `return`: the value after the colon is the answer. The lambda itself has no name. `half =` stores it in a variable, like any value.
It does the same job as this:
```python
def half(n):
    return n // 2
```
You call it the same way: `half(18)` is 9.
A lambda is handy when you hand a function over, with no `()`, like a dial for the resonance array, Mar'tu's machine that reads each hero: `run_array(roster, lambda hero: hero["mana"])`.
Two mistakes to watch for. A lambda can't hold `return`: Python stops with *invalid syntax*. And a lambda is one line only. For anything longer, or anything you'll use again, write a `def`. It has a name, and a name helps the next reader.

`run_array(heroes, dial)` is already finished: it calls `dial(hero)` for each hero and prints the reading. A hero's max mana is twice their magical affinity, how strong their magic is.

items.title: map(): One Function, Every Item
items.summary: Optional article. Hand `map()` a function and a list. It calls the function on every item and collects the answers.
items.body:
You've handed a function over before: `cast_on_everyone(roster, warm_hands)`. Python has a helper like that built in: [[map()]].
`map()` takes a function and a list. It calls the function on every item, in order, and collects what each call hands back. It's like an input-output table in math class: one rule, applied to every input.
```python
costs = [2, 6, 10]
doubled = list(map(double, costs))
```
Now `doubled` is `[4, 12, 20]`. Like `range()`, `map()` keeps its answers hidden until you wrap it in `list()`.
The function goes first, with no `()`, because `map()` does the calling. The list goes second. In the wrong order, Python stops with *'function' object is not iterable*: it can't go through a function item by item.
The function must hand back its answer with `return`. If it only prints, `map()` collects `None` for every item.
A [[lambda]] fits well here. The lambda article shows how: `list(map(lambda n: n * 2, costs))`.
`map()` saves you a loop. This does the same job:
```python
doubled = []
for cost in costs:
    doubled.append(double(cost))
```

items.title: Two Things Back
items.summary: Optional article. One function hands back two answers with `return share, spare`, and you catch both with `share, spare = ...`.
items.body:
Sometimes a function works out two answers. In math class, 17 ÷ 4 = 4 R 1 gives two answers at once: 4, and 1 left over. Lucky splits 17 coins among 4 heroes the same way: each gets 4, and 1 is left over. Why not hand back both?
Put a comma between them:
```python
return share, spare
```
Python packs the two values into a [[tuple]]: a few values in order, in parentheses, that can't change, like `(4, 1)`. The Tuples article in Unit 4 has more.
The line that called can catch both at once, one name for each, in order. Python calls that [[unpacking]]:
```python
share, spare = split_loot(17, 4)
```
Now `share` holds 4 and `spare` holds 1.
Three mistakes to watch for. Two `return` lines don't hand back two values: the first `return` ends the function, so the second never runs. One name on the left catches the whole tuple, `(4, 1)`. And the count must match: three names for two values stops Python with *not enough values to unpack*.

exercises.title: The bar's two numbers
exercises.martu:
A function can hand back two values at once. Put a comma between them: `return share, spare`. Python packs them into a [[tuple]], a pair in order, like a point (x, y) in math class. The line that called catches them with two names, in the same order: `full, empty = bar_parts(lucky)`. Python calls that [[unpacking]].
A mana bar needs two numbers: dark blocks for the mana Lucky has, and pale blocks for the mana used. `bar_parts` will hand back both.

anotherWay.label: Two values, one trip
anotherWay.text:
```text
return 20, 6
       |   |
     (20, 6)   one tuple
       |   |
full, empty = ...
```

anotherWay.label: Two bags from the market
anotherWay.text: You send someone to the market for bread and eggs. They come back once, carrying both. You take the bread in one hand and the eggs in the other, in the order you asked.

1. `bar_parts(lucky)` works out 20 and 26 - 20 = 6.
2. `return 20, 6` hands back the tuple `(20, 6)`.
3. `full, empty = ...` puts 20 in `full` and 6 in `empty`.
4. `"█" * 20 + "░" * 6` draws the bar.

anotherWay.label: Recap: tuples
anotherWay.text: A tuple is like a list in parentheses that can't change: `(20, 6)`. You can read it by position, `parts[0]`, or unpack it into names. The Tuples article in Unit 4 has more.

exercises.title: Learn a ward
exercises.martu:
`learn_ward` builds a ward, a spell that protects, from its parameters: one page for the book `wards`. Then it stores the page in the book under its name, like `add_spell` in the campaign. The book reads the keys `"mana_cost"` and `"effect"`, letter for letter. In the bottom call, a 0 holds the place where the effect goes. My check hands `learn_ward` other names, costs and effects.
Stuck? Skip this task, or go back to *Write the spell book* in the lesson Spells You Can Hand Over. Tasks you pass here stay ✓ done.

anotherWay.text:
1. `ward = {...}`: two keys in quotes, each holding the parameter of the same name, no quotes.
2. `wards[ward_name] = ward` stores it in the book that was handed in, under its name.
3. In the bottom call, `ash_ward` with no `()` hands the function itself over. With `()`, it would run right there.

items.title: Quick Check Recipes II · Form A questions
items.summary: Four questions that go with Quick Check Recipes II. To pass the Quick Check, get 3 of the 4 right.

questions.q: `cast_on_all` calls `effect(hero)` for each hero. Which line hands `shine` over, so it runs once for every hero?

whyWrong.0: With `()`, `shine` runs right now, before `cast_on_all` starts, with no hero. Python stops: *missing 1 required positional argument*.
whyWrong.2: `shine(lucky)` runs right now, for one hero only, and hands over its result, `None`. Then `cast_on_all` tries to call `None`, and Python stops: *'NoneType' object is not callable*.
whyWrong.3: In quotes, it's only text, and Python can't call text: *'str' object is not callable*.

questions.explain: The name with no `()` is the function itself. `cast_on_all` calls it later, once for each hero, with `effect(hero)`.

questions.q: Read the code. What will it print?
questions.explain: Inside, `print` shows 8. But the function has no `return`, so the call hands back `None`, and `total` holds `None`. To keep the 8, the function needs `return`.

questions.q: Read the code. What will it print?
questions.explain: `hero` and `oogrish` are two names for the same sheet, so the change reaches the line that called: 18 - 5 = 13. The function has no `return`, so `result` holds `None`. Changing a sheet needs no `return`.

questions.q: Read the code. What will it print?
questions.explain: The function built the key `"cost"`, and the last line asks for `"mana_cost"`. Python matches keys letter for letter, so it stops with a KeyError. The campaign reads `"mana_cost"`, so that is the key to build.

exercises.title: Learn a charm
exercises.martu:
`learn_charm` builds a charm, a spell that protects, from its parameters: one page for the book `charms`. Then it stores the page in the book under its name, like `add_spell` in the campaign. The book reads the keys `"mana_cost"` and `"effect"`, letter for letter. In the bottom call, a 0 holds the place where the effect goes. My check hands `learn_charm` other names, costs and effects.
Stuck? Skip this task, or go back to *Write the spell book* in the lesson Spells You Can Hand Over. Tasks you pass here stay ✓ done.

2. `charms[charm_name] = charm` stores it in the book that was handed in, under its name.
3. In the bottom call, `teal_shield` with no `()` hands the function itself over. With `()`, it would run right there.

items.summary: Four questions that go with Quick Check Recipes II. To pass the Quick Check, get 3 of the 4 right.

questions.q: `cast_on_all` calls `effect(hero)` for each hero. Which line hands `hum` over, so it runs once for every hero?

whyWrong.0: `hum(bomb_shell)` runs right now, for one hero only, and hands over its result, `None`. Then `cast_on_all` tries to call `None`, and Python stops: *'NoneType' object is not callable*.
whyWrong.1: In quotes, it's only text, and Python can't call text: *'str' object is not callable*.
whyWrong.3: With `()`, `hum` runs right now, before `cast_on_all` starts, with no hero. Python stops: *missing 1 required positional argument*.

questions.explain: The name with no `()` is the function itself. `cast_on_all` calls it later, once for each hero, with `effect(hero)`.

items.title: Mar'tu's Chalk Notes: Spell Recipes
items.summary: All of Unit 7 on one page. You can print it.

entries.concept: A function that takes a sheet
entries.note: The parameter `hero` is the sheet handed in. Read it by key, and hand back the answer with `return`. One function works for any sheet. You've seen this: `get_mana_bar(caster)`. Lesson: Recipes That Read Stat Sheets.

entries.concept: Changes to a sheet reach the line that called
entries.note: `hero` and `gearshift` are two names for the same sheet, so the line that called sees the change. No `return` is needed for that.
When the line that called needs a value back, like `mana_used`. A function that only changes a sheet, like `charge`, doesn't. With no `return`, a call hands back `None`.
The key `"mana_cost"` gets the parameter `mana_cost`, letter for letter, with no quotes. `"mana_cost": "mana_cost"` would store the letters mana_cost, not the cost. You've seen this: `add_spell`.
The key comes from the parameter, with no quotes. `book["rune_name"]` would make a page called rune_name, and `book = {...}` inside would make a new book the line that called never sees.
The guard goes first. `return` ends the call, so the lines below run only when the guard lets it through. You've seen this: the opening of `cast_spell`.

code: # Finished. Leave it as it is.
entries.note: Read its `def` line: what it takes, and in what order. Then call it that way, and change nothing inside it. You've seen this: `print_mana(caster, mana_bar)`.
Store what one function hands back in a variable, then pass that variable to the next. You've seen this: `show_mana(caster)`.
With no `()`, the name is the function itself: store it, or hand it over, and it runs later. `hush(...)` runs it now and hands back `None`. You've seen this: `strengthen_magic` with no `()`.
Read the page, then its `"effect"`, then call it: the parentheses on the end are what call it. Without them, nothing happens. You've seen this: `spell["spell_function"](caster)`.
A default is the usual value, used when the call hands over nothing. A keyword argument names the value, so the order doesn't matter. Extra practice: Defaults and Scope.

entries.concept: (extra) Variables inside a function stay there
entries.note: `flame` lives only inside `fill_lamp`, like scratch work. `print(flame)` outside stops with a NameError. Hand it back with `return`, and catch it outside.
A function on one line: the parameter, a colon, then what it hands back. No `def`, no `return`. Article: lambda.
Calls the function on every item and collects what each call hands back. The function goes first, with no `()`. Article: map().
A comma between two values hands back a tuple. Two names, in order, catch it. Article: Two Things Back.

entries.concept: Error: the call stored, then called
entries.note: TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable. In plain words: you tried to call `None`. `hush(...)` ran at once and stored `None`. Store the function itself: `chosen = hush`.
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "NoneType") to str. In plain words: you tried to glue `None` to text. `label` has no `return`, so the call hands back `None`.
TypeError: hush() missing 1 required positional argument: 'hero'. In plain words: `hush` got no hero. With `()`, it ran right away. Hand it over with no `()`.
KeyError: 'rune_name'. In plain words: the book has no key with those letters. In quotes, it's only the letters rune_name. Take the quotes off to use the parameter.

entries.concept: Error: a key that doesn't match
entries.note: KeyError: 'mana_cost'. In plain words: there's no key `"mana_cost"`. Keys match letter for letter, so build the key the reader asks for.

entries.concept: Error: a page called, not its effect
entries.note: TypeError: 'dict' object is not callable. In plain words: you tried to call a whole page. `runes["Hush"]` is the whole page. Read its `["effect"]` first, then call that.
